newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo govt to set bank reform framework by end 1997.
newsitem.headline: Yugo govt to set bank reform framework by end 1997.

text.p: Yugoslavia has vowed to establish a framework for bank reform by the end of 1997 and a senior government official has said the state would first bring in changes which did not require additional funding.

"Bank rehabilitation is clearly needed. It is also clear that any bank overhaul can't be conducted without additional funds. So we shall try to resolve some problems and prepare banks for a future overhaul," Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister Danko Djunic told Reuters over the weekend.

The government said on Friday it would step up activity to reform its ailing financial sector and transform the local financial market before privatisation in Serbia begins. It sees reform as crucial for further development of the sector.
The initial reforms will include a cleanup of massive bad debt in banks' balances and measures to ease the burden on banks of enormous frozen savings.
"We want banks with clean balances, without any bad debt," Djunic said.
Yugoslavia has 111 banks which together posted a 70 million dinars ($11.5 million) loss in 1996 with unrecoverable claims growing to 3.5 billion dinars.

The issue of bad debt, resulting from chronic illiquidity of the entire economy, was expected to be partially eased after six monthly rounds of the so-called multilateral compensation, a highly technical inter-company debt-settlement scheme, which is expected to reveal the true size of the internal debt.
Yugoslav banks are also burdened by almost $4 billion in private hard currency savings frozen in state banks since 1991.

Djunic said the government will discuss later this month a bill to release those savings. He suggested the state would resume responsibility not only for savings frozen in state banks but also for funds lost after a pyramid scheme run by Dafiment bank collapsed in April 1992.

"The government wants to solve the problem in a consistent way. The state must resolve the entire frozen savings issue and resume responsibility for savings in all financial institutions registered according to the law on banks," Djunic said.

Dafiment banka, although closed for five years, remains registered as a bank. Yugoslavs are estimated to have lost between 300 million and 500 million German marks ($270 million) with the Dafiment scheme.
According to the latest draft law, the state will recognize frozen savings as a public debt and issue bonds to service it.
The size of deposits the government plans to repay in cash remains unknown and depends on the state's financial resources.

But it is clear that the bonds, to be denominated in a hard currency, will be used for purchasing shares in Serbia's privatisation programme. Djunic also expected bonds to be traded on the secondary market.

"This is definitely a step forward in rehabilitating banks because they will be cleared from the liability. We shall score a point in developing the financial market and will also establish a close link with the privatisation scheme," he said.

Reforms will also lead to numerous mergers to adjust the oversized, inefficient sector to the country's needs. Once all the cleaning-up is finalised, some banks will either be forced to merge or dissappear.

"Concentration of the banking sector is inevitable. But it will strengthen the banks' capital base in a best possible way. Banks will merge, either in a natural way or the central bank will toughen criteria for founding banks, but one way or the other, there will be mergers," Djunic said.
The bank reform package will involve all banks.

Downsizing of the banking industry is bound to lead to massive lay-offs. Some 40 percent of bank employees were seen as surplus labour. But Djunic said the bank reform will be accompanied by a social programme.
($1 = 6.0941 Yugoslav dinars)
($ = 1.863 German Marks)
